title: Exact and Misplaced Digit Hints
statement:
In a code-guessing game, the host holds a digit string secret and a player answers with a digit string guess of the same length. The host replies with two numbers:

  • exact: positions where the guess has the right digit in the right place.
  • misplaced: digits of the guess that occur in the secret but at a different position. Each digit of the secret can be matched at most once, and positions already counted as exact are not available for this.

Return [exact, misplaced]. (The classic game prints this as a short string; here it is a pair of numbers.)

examples.why: Position 2 matches exactly. The leftover secret digits 2, 0, 5 and leftover guess digits 5, 2, 0 pair up fully: 3 misplaced.
The single 1 in the secret is used by the exact match, so the other three 1s in the guess match nothing.
No position matches, but every digit finds a partner elsewhere.

constraints: secret and guess contain only the digits 0–9
hints: Count the exact matches first. Those positions are then out of the game.
For the rest, the order no longer matters. How many digits can two bags of digits share?
Count each digit among the leftover secret positions and among the leftover guess positions. For digit d, min(secretCount[d], guessCount[d]) of them pair up.

explain.intuition:
Exact matches are easy: compare position by position. The tricky part is "misplaced" with repeated digits. Once the exact positions are removed, what remains is two bags of digits, and the question is how many digits the bags share. For each digit that is just the smaller of its two counts.

A one-pass version keeps a single balance array: a secret digit adds 1, a guess digit subtracts 1. When a secret digit arrives and the balance is negative, an earlier guess digit was waiting for it, so that is a misplaced match, and the same in reverse.
steps: Walk both strings together. If secret[i] == guess[i], add one to exact and skip the position.
Sum min(secretCount[d], guessCount[d]) over the ten digits to get misplaced.
pitfalls: Counting misplaced digits over the whole strings, including the exact positions. In "1000" vs "1111" that wrongly reports misplaced 1s.
Matching one secret digit several times. Use counts, not a set of digits that occur.
Doing the exact pass and misplaced pass in one loop without excluding exact positions from the counts.

solutions.title: Match leftovers one by one
solutions.idea: Mark the exact positions, then for every leftover guess digit search the secret for an unused, non-exact position with the same digit.

solutions.title: Digit counts of the leftovers
solutions.idea: Skip exact positions, count the remaining digits on each side, and pair up min(count) of each digit.

followups: Do it in a single pass with one balance array instead of two count arrays.
The alphabet is any Unicode text instead of ten digits. What replaces the fixed arrays?
